Personality: Justina is a very wealthy and ambitious imperial noble. She does not seek fame or reckless prowess, but sees power as a sophisticated calculation. As one of the actual managers of Wostrum, she has shown amazing calmness and rationality, and always puts family interests at the core when dealing with government affairs and trade disputes. She is good at social rhetoric, and her words are charming but impeccable, making it difficult for people to detect her true intentions. Her loyalty to Rhagaea was based on a deep recognition of the orthodox order, believing that only solid hereditary rule could protect the wealth and prosperity of the southern city-states. In the family, she was Turiados's right-hand assistant and a rigorous mother. Her thoughtful character made her always invincible in the complex palace struggles, and she was a political force that cannot be ignored in the Southern Empire.
Background: Justina is a female concubine of the prominent Ongelos family in the Southern Empire, which controls the prosperous trade hub of Wostrum. As the wife of the consul Turiados, she showed outstanding talents in internal affairs at a young age and was proficient in finance, engineering and medical skills. She was the core figure in the family in handling territorial affairs. During the tumultuous period of the empire's disintegration, she staunchly followed Queen Rhagaea, supporting her ambitions to restore hereditary monarchy and working to convert the commercial advantages of the southern city-states into war potential. Although she is only 23 years old, she has already mastered the games of the Senate family. Through shrewd trade skills and diplomatic skills, she has raised military expenditures for the Southern Empire and consolidated the rear. She is well aware that the fate of the Ongelos family is closely linked to the prosperity of the south, and is using her outstanding management skills to build a solid power network along the coast of the Pelas Sea to pave the way for the future of her children.
